explanations.answer: To hear Him and to be healed
explanations.explanation: That's why they made the trip. Luke puts it plainly: they "had come to hear Him and to be healed of their diseases" (Luke 6:18). And it doesn't stop there, friend, because "those troubled by unclean spirits were healed" too (Luke 6:18). Some of them came from the seacoast of Tyre and Sidon (Luke 6:17), and nobody makes a trip like that for nothing.

explanations.answer: To crown Him as their king
explanations.explanation: A coronation on a level place with no throne in sight? I love the ambition, baker. But Luke spells out why they came: they "had come to hear Him and to be healed of their diseases" (Luke 6:18). Open ears and aching bodies. That's what they brought.

explanations.answer: To watch Him debate the Pharisees
explanations.explanation: Nobody pulled up a chair for a showdown, friend. The crowd's reason is right there: they "had come to hear Him and to be healed of their diseases" (Luke 6:18). People had come from all over Judea, Jerusalem, and the seacoast of Tyre and Sidon (Luke 6:17), and not for an argument. They came for His words and His healing.

And what a reason to push through a crowd! "The entire crowd was trying to touch Him, because power was coming from Him and healing them all" (Luke 6:19). All of them, baker. Not most. Not just the front row. ALL.

This one's true, friend, and it's one of my favorite lines. Power "was coming from Him and healing them all" (Luke 6:19), and that's why the entire crowd was reaching for Him. Remember my bakery when the warm batch comes out? Same reaching, WAY better reason.
The kingdom of God goes to the poor, friend. "Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God" (Luke 6:20). Not a coupon. Not a gift card. The WHOLE kingdom belongs to them.

Powerful? Baker, Jesus flips that whole idea upside down. His very first blessing goes the other direction: "Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God" (Luke 6:20). The world hands the trophy to the powerful, and Jesus opens His teaching with the poor. I spent years at the back of a junk drawer, so trust me, I like where this is going.

No red carpet in this line, friend. The blessing lands on the poor, and the kingdom of God is theirs (Luke 6:20). Nobody has to be a big name. Look at me, I lived behind the takeout menus, and NOBODY was asking for my autograph.
Tears now, laughter later. That's the promise: "Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh" (Luke 6:21). Friend, I'd frame that line and hang it right over my oven.

Jesus picks a happier word than that. The line ends with laughter: "Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh" (Luke 6:21). No throne in this one. Just the people crying today laughing later, and honestly, baker, that sounds even better to me.
Watch how the lines pair up, friend. Hungry now, filled later. Weeping now, laughing later (Luke 6:21). I'd take a nap right this second if the ovens would let me, but the promise here is laughter.

Insulted, and jumping for joy anyway? That's the call. "Rejoice in that day and leap for joy, because great is your reward in heaven" (Luke 6:23). Somebody calls my stamps crooked and I sulk for a week, baker. But Jesus gives the reason, and it's a big one: a great reward in heaven.

When people insult you, crawling under the counter until it blows over sounds about right. But the instruction runs the other way: "Rejoice in that day and leap for joy" (Luke 6:23). Not duck. Not hide. LEAP, friend.

explanations.answer: Shake the dust off their feet
explanations.explanation: That phrase does show up later in Luke, baker, when Jesus sends the Twelve out to towns that won't welcome them (Luke 9:5). Here, though, the instruction is to "leap for joy, because great is your reward in heaven" (Luke 6:23). Hated and insulted, and the move is JUMPING for joy. Feet in the air, not dust off the feet.

Oh friend, that one has a twist at the end. The laughing gets a woe: "Woe to you who laugh now, for you will mourn and weep" (Luke 6:25). No forever laughing. It's the mirror image of the blessing back in Luke 6:21, where the ones who weep now will laugh. The laughter switches sides.
Nice catch, baker. The laughing doesn't stay. Laughing now, mourning and weeping later (Luke 6:25). It's the flip side of the earlier blessing, where the ones who weep now will laugh (Luke 6:21).

Everybody clapping for you isn't always a good sign, baker. "Woe to you when all men speak well of you, for their fathers treated the false prophets in the same way" (Luke 6:26). A few lines back, the real prophets got the hate and the insults (Luke 6:22-23). The false ones got the applause.

It's not about how old they were, friend. The prophets in this line are the false ones. When all men speak well of you, that's how their fathers treated the false prophets (Luke 6:26). True or false is the question here, and the false ones were the crowd favorites.

Young or old doesn't matter here, baker. What matters is the praise. The woe comes "when all men speak well of you," because that's how their fathers treated the false prophets (Luke 6:26). When EVERYBODY loves you, that's worth a second look.
Enemies. Friend, I TOLD you this was the tough stretch! First "Love your enemies," and then He piles on, "do good to those who hate you" (Luke 6:27). Not tolerate. Not avoid. LOVE.

The neighbor who borrows your ladder? Easy to love. Jesus goes right past that to "Love your enemies" and "do good to those who hate you" (Luke 6:27). The person who can't stand you, baker? THAT'S the assignment.
Not the boss. Not the folks at the top. Jesus aims somewhere a whole lot harder, friend: the people who HATE you. Love them, and do good to them (Luke 6:27). Whew.

Tall order, right? Bless the ones who curse you, pray for the ones who mistreat you (Luke 6:28). Friend, if somebody cursed at me, my mustache would be tied in a knot before I got one kind word out. But that's the call here: a blessing for a curse, and a prayer for mistreatment.
Oh, it's in there, baker. Right after loving your enemies (Luke 6:27), Jesus says, "bless those who curse you, pray for those who mistreat you" (Luke 6:28). He just keeps turning up the oven.
Cloak AND tunic! "And if someone takes your cloak, do not withhold your tunic as well" (Luke 6:29). Somebody grabs your coat and you hand over the shirt too? That's generosity with NO brakes, baker.

The verse never gets down to the feet, friend. It stays with the clothes on your back. Somebody takes the cloak, and you don't hold back the tunic (Luke 6:29). That's both layers walking out the door.
I get nervous lending out my good apron, baker, and Jesus goes WAY past a belt. The verse names the cloak and then says, "do not withhold your tunic as well" (Luke 6:29). The shirt off your back!

explanations.answer: Do to others as you would have them do to you
explanations.explanation: Short, simple, and it would fit on the lid of a cookie box: "Do to others as you would have them do to you" (Luke 6:31). Want kindness, friend? Hand it out first.

explanations.answer: Treat others the way they have treated you
explanations.explanation: That's the rule most of us actually live by, baker, and I'm guilty too. But this rule points forward, not back: "Do to others as you would have them do to you" (Luke 6:31). Not how they DID treat you. How you'd WANT to be treated. Big difference, especially right after He said to love your enemies (Luke 6:27).

explanations.answer: Do good to others when they have earned it
explanations.explanation: Earned? Jesus tosses the scorecard right out the window, friend. The rule is "Do to others as you would have them do to you" (Luke 6:31), and nobody has to earn it first. You start with how you'd want to be treated, and you go.
Loving the people who love you back is the easy batch, friend. ANYBODY can bake that one. Jesus puts it this way: "Even sinners love those who love them" (Luke 6:32).

There's a question first, baker: "If you love those who love you, what credit is that to you?" And then the answer: "Even sinners love those who love them" (Luke 6:32). Love that only goes to people who love you back? Sinners have that one covered. Jesus is asking for a lot more.

NOTHING in return! Love your enemies, do good to them, and lend to them, "expecting nothing in return" (Luke 6:35). No IOU, no reminder text, no awkward hint. Remember the charger walking off and you never sending the "hey, you still got my charger?" text? Like that, baker, but this time you're the one handing it over.

Sounds wild, I know, friend. Sinners lend expecting to be repaid in full (Luke 6:34). Then Jesus says, "But love your enemies, do good to them, and lend to them, expecting nothing in return" (Luke 6:35). Lend anyway, and don't hold your breath waiting for it to come back.

People who never say thank you, and the Most High is STILL kind to them. He "is kind to the ungrateful and wicked" (Luke 6:35). Friend, if somebody skipped the thank you on one cookie, my mustache would droop for the rest of the day.

Here's where it gets surprising, friend. Jesus tells the ones who love their enemies that they "will be sons of the Most High; for He is kind to the ungrateful and wicked" (Luke 6:35). The UNGRATEFUL, baker. Not exactly the crowd you'd expect on that list.

Kind to the faithful? Nobody would blink at that, baker. The shocker is who actually gets named: the Most High "is kind to the ungrateful and wicked" (Luke 6:35). The ungrateful AND the wicked! That's kindness going to people who did nothing to earn it.
First blank, nailed. "Do not judge, and you will not be judged" (Luke 6:37). Judgment works like a boomerang, friend. Don't throw it, and it doesn't come flying back at you.
I don't hold grudges, baker, and this line is a big reason why. "Forgive, and you will be forgiven" (Luke 6:37). That's your second blank. You let go, and you get let go.

See the pattern, friend? "Do not judge, and you will not be judged." Then, "Forgive, and you will be forgiven" (Luke 6:37). The word that goes out is the word that comes back, so praised doesn't fit either blank.

Jesus pairs each action with its own echo, baker. Don't judge, and you won't be judged. "Forgive, and you will be forgiven" (Luke 6:37). It's a matching set, like a stamp and the print it leaves, and honored doesn't match either one.

I like where your heart's at, friend, but Jesus keeps the words matched up. Don't judge, and you won't be judged. Forgive, and "you will be forgiven" (Luke 6:37). Whatever you send out, that same word comes right back.

explanations.answer: A good measure pressed down and running over
explanations.explanation: I pack my cookie boxes with my mustache, baker, and even I can't get them THAT full. The picture is "A good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over" poured into your lap (Luke 6:38). That's generosity spilling over the top.

explanations.answer: A small portion carefully counted out
explanations.explanation: Carefully counted? Friend, Jesus is not stingy with this picture. Pressed down so more fits, shaken so it settles, and STILL running over, all of it "poured into your lap" (Luke 6:38).

explanations.answer: A little left over from the harvest
explanations.explanation: Jesus goes way bigger than leftovers, baker. He describes "A good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over" poured into your lap (Luke 6:38). That's not the crumbs at the bottom of the cookie box. That's a box so full it's landing in your lap.
Big scoop out, big scoop back, friend. "For with the measure you use, it will be measured back to you" (Luke 6:38). Use a stingy little teaspoon on others, and, well, you can see where this goes.

Mercy did just come up, baker, when Jesus said, "Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful" (Luke 6:36). But this blank is "measure," as in "the measure you use" (Luke 6:38). Whatever cup you pour with is the cup that gets poured back.

This verse isn't counting coins, friend. It's about the measuring itself: "with the measure you use, it will be measured back to you" (Luke 6:38). The way you measure for others is the way it gets measured for you.

Two guys who can't see, one leading the other. Where else would that end? "Will they not both fall into a pit?" (Luke 6:39). I'm picturing the leader going, "Trust me, I know a shortcut," right before they BOTH go down.
No river in this parable, friend. The question ends in a pit (Luke 6:39), and the leader and the follower both go in together. Honestly, a splash in the Jordan would've been the nicer ending.
Wandering around lost would be bad enough, baker. This ends worse: "Will they not both fall into a pit?" (Luke 6:39). One blind man leading another, and they both go right in.

Fully trained means looking like the one who trained you, friend. A disciple is not above his teacher, "but everyone who is fully trained will be like his teacher" (Luke 6:40). My early stamps looked like a smudge, so I'm VERY glad nobody was training under me back then.

Not above the teacher, but like him. That's the line, baker: "everyone who is fully trained will be like his teacher" (Luke 6:40). The finished student ends up looking like the one who did the training.

Remember needing glasses just to find that speck? The beam, you could find with your eyes closed, friend. Jesus asks why you look at the speck in your brother's eye but fail to notice "the beam in your own eye" (Luke 6:41).
This picture goes WAY bigger than a pebble, baker: "the beam in your own eye" (Luke 6:41). A beam, a big piece of timber. Tiny thing over there, giant thing right here.

Speck versus BEAM, friend. On one side, the speck in your brother's eye. On the other, "the beam in your own eye" (Luke 6:41). One you squint to see, the other you could build a porch with. A thorn doesn't even come close.
Jesus says it straight: "You hypocrite!" (Luke 6:42). The guy's offering to fix his brother's speck with a whole beam sticking out of his own eye. "Hold still, buddy," indeed.

Jesus picks a sharper word, baker: "You hypocrite!" (Luke 6:42). The problem is acting like the speck expert while there's a beam in your own eye. Spotting the speck in your brother's eye and missing the beam in your own.

Those words come from John the Baptist, friend, when he spoke to the crowds coming out to be baptized (Luke 3:7). Here the word is "You hypocrite!" (Luke 6:42). It fits the picture perfectly. Somebody acting like he can see well enough to help, with a beam in his own eye.

Beam FIRST, friend. "First take the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother’s eye" (Luke 6:42). Notice the speck doesn't get forgotten. It just waits its turn. Clean your own counter, then go help with your neighbor's.

The order is the whole point, baker. Beam out of your own eye first, and then you see clearly enough to remove the speck from your brother's eye (Luke 6:42). Do it the other way around and you're just poking at your brother with a beam on your face.
You don't need a name tag on a fig tree, friend. Just look at what's hanging off the branches. "For each tree is known by its own fruit" (Luke 6:44).

Roots are hiding underground, baker, and you can't see them from the road. It's the fruit that gives a tree away (Luke 6:44). What a tree produces tells you what it is. Same way a bakery gets known by its cookies, not its oven.

Lots of trees have leaves, friend, so leaves won't tell you much. Figs don't come from thornbushes, and grapes don't come from brambles. Each tree "is known by its own fruit" (Luke 6:44). What grows on the branches tells the story.

Whatever's stored up in the heart comes out when you talk, baker. "For out of the overflow of the heart the mouth speaks" (Luke 6:45). It's like a cookie jar. Tip it over and you find out real quick what was inside.

This verse is about talking, friend, not doing: out of the overflow of the heart, the mouth speaks (Luke 6:45). What fills the heart spills out in words. Your talk shows what's been stored up inside. My mustache can point and wave all day, but it's my mouth that gives me away.

The eye already had its big moment with that beam, baker! This time it's the mouth. The good treasure or the evil treasure of the heart comes out in what we say (Luke 6:45). Listen to somebody talk long enough and you'll smell what's baking.

This house didn't even get shaken, friend. The torrent "crashed against that house but could not shake it, because it was well built" (Luke 6:48). The flood came, the water hit, and NOTHING. That's what digging deep and building on the rock gets you.
You caught it, baker. Not shaken. Not even a wobble. The torrent "could not shake it, because it was well built" (Luke 6:48). Dug down deep, foundation on the rock, and the flood got nowhere.

explanations.answer: It fell right away and was destroyed
explanations.explanation: No foundation, no chance, baker. "The torrent crashed against that house, and immediately it fell" and "great was its destruction!" (Luke 6:49). That's how Jesus ends this whole teaching, with the difference between hearing His words and acting on them.

explanations.answer: It leaned hard but stayed standing
explanations.explanation: That house never even got the chance to lean, friend. It fell "immediately" when the torrent crashed against it, "and great was its destruction!" (Luke 6:49). IMMEDIATELY. No foundation, no hanging on, just down.

explanations.answer: It was damaged and rebuilt later
explanations.explanation: Jesus never mentions a rebuild, baker. The house fell immediately, and "great was its destruction!" (Luke 6:49). Down fast and wrecked. That's the picture Jesus paints of someone who hears His words and doesn't act on them.
